The word "urchin" has two main meanings in modern English, and one older, rarer meaning that you might still come across in old books.
Meaning 1: A Mischievous or Poorly-Dressed Child

The most common everyday use of "urchin" refers to a child — usually a small boy — who is scruffy, poorly dressed, and often up to some mischief. The word carries a sense of the child being a little wild, cheeky, or hard to control. Importantly, the word is not purely negative. It often has a certain warmth or even affection behind it, as if the speaker finds the child troublesome but also a little charming.

You might picture a barefoot kid with dirty clothes, a cheeky grin, and no adult watching over them — that is the classic image of an urchin.

Example: "A gang of little urchins were running through the market, stealing apples and laughing."

A very common phrase you will encounter is "street urchin." This specifically refers to a child who lives or spends most of their time on the streets, often without a stable home or proper care. Street urchins are associated with poverty, neglect, and having to fend for themselves. The phrase is widely used in literature, especially in stories set in the past — think of Victorian-era novels where orphaned children roam city streets.

Example: "He had grown up as a street urchin, sleeping in doorways and surviving on scraps."

In tone, calling someone an urchin is rarely a harsh insult. It is more of a colourful, slightly old-fashioned way of describing a rough-around-the-edges, rowdy child. Adults sometimes use it with a smile, almost fondly, when a child is being naughty but in a harmless, endearing way.

Example: "Come here, you little urchin! You've got mud all over the floor again."
Meaning 2: A Sea Urchin (A Marine Animal)

"Urchin" is also the short form of sea urchin, which is a real sea creature. In everyday speech and writing, people often just say "urchin" to mean a sea urchin, especially in contexts related to the ocean, marine biology, or food.

A sea urchin is a small, round animal that lives on the ocean floor. Its body is covered all over with sharp, pointed spines sticking out in every direction, which gives it the look of a spiky ball. These spines protect it from predators. Beneath the spines, the body is round and hard, like a shell.

Sea urchins eat algae and other plant matter, and they move slowly across rocks and the seabed. They come in various colours — purple, red, black, green, and more.

Example: "Be careful where you step on the reef — there are urchins hiding among the rocks."

Sea urchins are also eaten as food in many parts of the world. The edible part is actually the creature's reproductive organs (called "roe"), which have a rich, creamy, ocean-like flavour. In Japanese cuisine, they are a prized ingredient called "uni."

Example: "The chef served a dish of fresh pasta topped with sea urchin."

In very old English — and you will mainly see this in classic literature or historical texts — "urchin" was used to mean a hedgehog. This meaning is largely obsolete today, but it is worth knowing so that you are not confused if you come across it in an old poem or play. Nobody in modern conversation uses "urchin" to mean a hedgehog.

Think of it this way: both the child and the sea creature share something in common. A sea urchin is spiky, a little wild, and unpredictable. A child called an urchin is similarly rough, unruly, and hard to handle. The word captures a kind of untamed, prickly quality in both cases — one literally (the animal's spines), and one figuratively (the child's behaviour).

When you see the word "urchin" alone in a modern sentence, context will almost always tell you which meaning is intended. If the sentence is about the sea, beaches, or marine life, it means the animal. If it is about children, streets, or people, it means a scruffy, mischievous kid.
